red.focus: Distinguish a legal source from a sound argument
red.summary: An argument can be logically well formed but based on a false premise, and a true premise can be used badly. Learn to ask whether reasoning follows and whether its sources are actually authoritative.
checklist: I can identify premise and conclusion
I can recognize when a conclusion follows from stated assumptions
I can check whether a legal premise is supported by a source

sections.title: An Argument Has Parts
sections.body_md: A lawyer says: 'Every validly licensed driver may use this road. Ada has a valid license. Therefore Ada may use this road.' The first two sentences are premises; the last is the conclusion. If the premises are true and no exception applies, the reasoning has a clear structure. Legal analysis begins by identifying those parts rather than being impressed by confidence or eloquence. A clear argument makes it possible to test where a conclusion might fail.

sections.title: Valid Reasoning and True Premises
sections.body_md: A deductive argument is valid when its conclusion must be true if the premises are true. An argument is sound when it is valid and its premises are actually true. A fabricated statute can supply the premise of a perfectly valid argument without making the legal advice correct. Lawyers must therefore check logic and authority separately. This distinction prevents a polished chain of reasoning from disguising an unsupported legal claim.

sections.title: The Law Supplies Conditions
sections.body_md: Real legal rules often contain definitions, exceptions and limits that simplified syllogisms omit. The premise 'every licensed driver may use this road' might be false during an emergency closure. Before applying logic, locate the actual rule and relevant facts. Then reconstruct the argument with its qualifications. Legal reasoning is not simply formal mathematics; it uses accurate sources and facts to decide which premises deserve acceptance. A good lawyer never lets an elegant form replace a necessary source check.

yellow.focus: Analyze legal syllogisms and conditional reasoning
yellow.summary: Learn how to express a rule as conditions and apply it accurately. Distinguish affirming a consequence from proving the condition that produced it.
checklist: I can construct a simple legal syllogism
I can recognize affirming the consequent
I can identify a missing statutory condition

sections.title: The Legal Syllogism
sections.body_md: Suppose an ordinance states that anyone operating a business in a specified zone must obtain a permit. A person operates a business in that zone. It follows that the ordinance requires a permit, assuming the rule is in force and no exception applies. This is a legal syllogism: a general rule, a factual premise and a conclusion. Its quality depends on accurately stating both premises and respecting qualifications. The logic helps organize the law, not discover the law's content.
sections.audio_script: Suppose an ordinance states that anyone operating a business in a specified zone must obtain a permit. A person operates a business in that zone. It follows that the ordinance requires a permit, assuming the rule is in force and no exception applies. This is a legal syllogism: a general rule, a factual premise and a conclusion. Its quality depends on accurately stating both premises and respecting qualifications. The logic helps organize the law, not discover the law's content.

sections.title: The Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent
sections.body_md: If an unlicensed shop violates a permit rule, that does not mean every shop accused of violating the rule is unlicensed. The form 'If P, then Q; Q; therefore P' is invalid. Q could arise for other reasons. Legal arguments sometimes commit this error when they infer wrongdoing solely from a bad outcome. A patient may suffer injury after treatment without proving malpractice. The existence of a consequence does not establish the particular conduct alleged to have caused it.

A patient may suffer injury after treatment without proving malpractice. The existence of a consequence does not establish the particular conduct alleged to have caused it.

sections.title: Find the Conditions Not Mentioned
sections.body_md: A statute may require a permit only for businesses operating more than a specified number of days or may exempt certain activities. A simplified syllogism that omits these conditions may reach the wrong result. Before reasoning, make an element chart and mark exceptions. Then ask which facts satisfy each condition. A valid inference with an incomplete legal premise can still be unsound. Precise argument requires fidelity to the actual rule's structure.

orange.focus: Distinguish deductive, inductive and abductive legal reasoning
orange.summary: Legal work often draws conclusions from incomplete evidence rather than strict deduction. Learn how inductive generalization and inference to the best explanation differ from a logically necessary conclusion.
checklist: I can compare deduction, induction and abduction
I can evaluate evidence strength without exaggeration
I can identify plausible rival explanations

sections.title: Deduction Gives Conditional Necessity
sections.body_md: A properly formed deduction tells us that if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. But most disputed legal facts are not established that way. A witness may support an event without proving it with logical certainty. A criminal standard such as beyond reasonable doubt is a legal standard of proof, not a formal theorem that removes all conceivable uncertainty. A lawyer should identify when logic provides necessity and when evidence supports a degree of confidence.
sections.audio_script: A properly formed deduction tells us that if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. But most disputed legal facts are not established that way. A witness may support an event without proving it with logical certainty. A criminal standard such as beyond reasonable doubt is a legal standard of proof, not a formal theorem that removes all conceivable uncertainty. A lawyer should identify when logic provides necessity and when evidence supports a degree of confidence.

sections.title: Induction Learns From Observations
sections.body_md: An analyst reviews many comparable cases and notices that courts usually treat a particular factor as significant. This may inform prediction but does not establish a binding universal rule. The sample may exclude unpublished decisions or differ from the client's jurisdiction. Inductive reasoning generalizes from observed instances; it is sensitive to representativeness and counterexamples. A reliable argument reports how cases were selected and distinguishes legal authority from empirical prediction.

A reliable argument reports how cases were selected and distinguishes legal authority from empirical prediction.

sections.title: Abduction Seeks the Best Explanation
sections.body_md: A window is broken, security footage shows a person nearby, and glass fragments are found on their clothing. The investigator may infer that this person broke the window, but other explanations are possible. Abduction chooses a proposed explanation that best fits the evidence. Legal reasoning must test alternatives, credibility and the required standard of proof. Presenting an abductive inference as a deductive certainty hides the uncertainty that fair adjudication must assess.

black.focus: Critique formalization and defeasible legal reasoning
black.summary: At doctoral depth, explain why legal rules often operate with exceptions and priorities that pure deductive logic does not capture. Defend rigor without concealing contested premises or institutional choice.
checklist: I can explain defeasible inference in law
I can evaluate rule conflicts and priority structures
I can distinguish formal validity from warranted legal conclusion

sections.title: Legal Rules Are Often Defeasible
sections.body_md: A general legal rule may state that an act is prohibited, yet another rule creates a justified exception. The ordinary conclusion can be defeated by new information about necessity, consent or an authorized exemption. Defeasible reasoning models conclusions that hold unless specified countervailing facts appear. It differs from an inconsistency in the actual law. A rigorous theory should identify the rule, exception and legal priority rather than simply treating every qualification as a reason logic is useless.
sections.audio_script: A general legal rule may state that an act is prohibited, yet another rule creates a justified exception. The ordinary conclusion can be defeated by new information about necessity, consent or an authorized exemption. Defeasible reasoning models conclusions that hold unless specified countervailing facts appear. It differs from an inconsistency in the actual law. A rigorous theory should identify the rule, exception and legal priority rather than simply treating every qualification as a reason logic is useless.

sections.title: Formal Systems Have Inputs
sections.body_md: Automated rule engines can encode statutory conditions and produce consistent results when their inputs and rules are accurate. Yet a model may misclassify a person, omit a valid exception or use outdated law. Logical correctness inside a formal system does not establish the legitimacy of the encoded legal premises. A doctoral critique examines rule provenance, interpretive uncertainty, procedural challenge and methods for correcting errors. A perfectly executed bad rule can still cause serious injustice.

sections.title: The Normative Choice Remains Visible
sections.body_md: When two legal principles conflict, courts may need a recognized priority rule, balancing method or interpretive judgment. Formal logic can clarify the structure but cannot supply every moral or institutional premise. A strong legal argument states which conclusions follow from accepted rules and which depend on contested interpretation. This transparency respects both intellectual rigor and the rule of law. It also protects clients from false certainty generated by sophisticated notation.
